definition: The smallest living unit. All living organisms are built up of cells. A human body contains roughly 37 trillion cells of many different types.
A membrane-bound structure inside the cell that contains the genetic material (DNA). The nucleus controls the cell's activities and acts as a control centre.
Deoxyribonucleic acid - the chemical substance that carries genetic information. DNA consists of a double helix of nucleotides with the bases adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C).
DNA's three-dimensional shape - two nucleotide strands that spiral around each other. The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: A pairs with T, and G pairs with C.
A tightly coiled DNA molecule surrounded by proteins. Humans have 46 chromosomes in most cells, organised into 23 pairs. Sex cells have only 23 chromosomes.
An ordinary body chromosome that is not a sex chromosome. Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes (chromosomes 1-22), the same in both sexes. The genes on the autosomes control most of the body's traits.
The chromosome that determines an individual's biological sex. Humans have two sex chromosomes: X and Y. Someone with XX typically develops as female, and someone with XY as male.

The two chromosomes in a pair, which carry the same set of genes in the same order - one inherited from the mother and one from the father. They are the same length and carry alleles for the same traits, but the alleles can differ. (X and Y in men are an exception and are not fully homologous.)

The building block of DNA. Each nucleotide consists of a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base (A, T, G or C). Nucleotides link together in long chains that form the DNA strand.

The part of a nucleotide that carries the actual genetic information. DNA has four nitrogenous bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). In RNA, thymine is replaced by uracil (U). The order of the bases forms the cell's code.

A pair of complementary bases that bond to each other in the DNA double helix: adenine (A) binds to thymine (T), and guanine (G) binds to cytosine (C). The base-pairing rule means each DNA strand can be used as a template for copying.
A defined sequence of DNA that contains instructions for building a specific protein. Humans have an estimated 20,000-25,000 protein-coding genes.
The fixed position on a chromosome where a specific gene is located. The loci (plural) of homologous chromosomes carry the alleles of the same gene.
The complete set of DNA in an organism's cells - all the chromosomes and all the genes. The human genome contains about 3 billion base pairs.
One of the alternative forms of a gene that can occur at a specific locus on a chromosome. Every person has two alleles of each gene - one from the mother and one from the father.
An allele whose trait shows up in the phenotype even if the individual has only one copy of it. Written with a capital letter, e.g. A.
An allele whose trait only shows up in the phenotype if the individual has two copies of it (homozygous). Written with a lowercase letter, e.g. a.
When both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote. Example: blood type AB, where both the A and B alleles are expressed at the same time on red blood cells.

An inheritance pattern where the heterozygous individual gets a blend between the two homozygous phenotypes. If, for example, a red flower and a white flower are crossed and the offspring turns out pink, the inheritance is incomplete - neither allele is fully dominant over the other. Also called intermediate inheritance.

The most common system for dividing blood into groups, based on which molecules sit on the red blood cells. The genes give the blood types A, B, AB and 0. The A and B alleles are codominant, while 0 is recessive. The system is crucial for blood transfusions.

A blood group system that shows whether a particular molecule, the Rh factor, is present on the red blood cells. Someone who has it is Rh-positive (Rh+), and someone who lacks it is Rh-negative (Rh−). The Rh factor matters for blood transfusions and during pregnancy.
An individual's genetic makeup, i.e. which alleles they carry. Written e.g. AA, Aa or aa. The genotype is not always visible from the outside.
The observable appearance and measurable traits of an organism, determined by the genotype and environmental influence. Examples: eye colour, blood type, height.
An individual with two identical alleles of a gene (AA or aa).
An individual with two different alleles of a gene (Aa). Also called a carrier if the recessive allele can cause disease when present in double copy.
An individual who is heterozygous (Aa) for a recessive disease allele. The carrier is healthy but can pass the disease allele on to their children.
Ribonucleic acid - a molecular intermediate in the flow of information from DNA to protein. RNA is single-stranded and uses the base uracil (U) instead of thymine (T).
The first step in protein synthesis. In the nucleus, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads the DNA sequence and creates a complementary mRNA molecule.
Messenger RNA. A single-stranded RNA molecule that is a copy of a gene and carries the instructions from the nucleus to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
A small structure in the cytoplasm that reads mRNA and assembles proteins from amino acids. Often called the cell's protein factory.
The second step in protein synthesis. The ribosome reads the mRNA sequence codon by codon and links amino acids together in the right order to form a protein.
A sequence of three bases in mRNA that codes for a specific amino acid. For example, AUG (the start codon) codes for the amino acid methionine. There are 64 possible codons for 20 amino acids.
The building block of proteins. There are 20 different amino acids. The order of amino acids in a protein determines the protein's three-dimensional shape and function.
Transfer RNA. A carrier molecule that brings the correct amino acid to the ribosome during translation. Each tRNA has an anticodon that pairs with a codon on the mRNA.

A sequence of three bases on tRNA that is complementary to a specific codon on mRNA. The base-pairing between the anticodon and the codon ensures that the correct amino acid is added during translation.
The universal system that links triplets of mRNA bases (codons) to amino acids. The code is essentially universal - nearly identical in all living organisms, which points to a common origin.
The overall process by which the cell builds a protein based on the information in DNA. Happens in two steps: transcription (DNA to mRNA) and translation (mRNA to protein).

A type of cell division in which a cell divides to form two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell (46 in humans). Used for growth and repair.
A type of cell division that produces sex cells (eggs and sperm) with half the number of chromosomes (23). Meiosis creates genetic variation through recombination and independent assortment.

A sex cell, i.e. an egg cell or a sperm cell. Gametes are haploid and carry only one set of chromosomes (23 in humans). When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, a new individual with a full set of chromosomes is formed.
A cell with a single set of chromosomes (n). Human sex cells are haploid, with 23 chromosomes. At fertilisation, two haploid cells fuse to form one diploid cell.

The very first cell of a new individual, formed when a sperm fertilises an egg cell. The zygote is diploid because it has received one set of chromosomes from each parent. The whole organism grows from the zygote through repeated cell divisions.
A cell with two copies of each chromosome (2n). Most cells in the body are diploid, with 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). Written as 2n = 46 for humans.
The exchange of chromosome segments between homologous chromosomes during meiosis. Creates new combinations of alleles (recombinants) and is an important source of genetic variation.
A permanent change in the DNA sequence. Can occur spontaneously, or be caused by radiation or chemicals. Most mutations have little effect, but some can lead to disease or change traits.
A grid used to predict the probability of different genotypes and phenotypes in offspring, given the parents' genotypes. Invented by the geneticist Reginald Punnett.

A cross in which two traits are followed at the same time, i.e. two genes at once. In a cross diagram, two heterozygous parents (e.g. AaBb x AaBb) produce several different combinations in the offspring. Shows how different traits can be inherited independently of each other.

Inheritance of traits whose gene is located on an autosome (a non-sex chromosome, chromosome pairs 1-22). Affects men and women equally. Can be dominant (one copy is enough) or recessive (requires two copies).

Inheritance of traits whose genes are located on the sex chromosomes (X or Y). Since men have XY and women XX, sex-linked traits (e.g. colour blindness) are often passed on differently in the two sexes.

A common sex-linked trait in which the eye has difficulty distinguishing certain colours, usually red and green. The trait is recessive and located on the X chromosome, which means men are affected considerably more often than women - after all, a man has only one X chromosome.

A diagram showing how a trait or disease is inherited through several generations in a family. Women are usually drawn as circles and men as squares, and filled-in symbols show who has the trait. Used to work out the pattern of inheritance and who are carriers.

The interplay between genetic factors (heredity) and environmental factors that together determine an individual's traits. Most complex traits - such as height and intelligence - are influenced by both.
A visual image of an individual's complete set of chromosomes, arranged in numerical order. Used to detect chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).
An individual has three copies of a chromosome instead of the normal two. Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome. Occurs when chromosome separation fails during meiosis (non-disjunction).

A condition caused by a person having three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two (trisomy 21). The extra chromosome affects development and appearance and often brings certain learning difficulties. It usually arises from an error when the sex cells are formed.
A disease caused by changes in the genetic material. Can be inherited (e.g. cystic fibrosis, phenylketonuria) or arise from a new mutation (e.g. Down syndrome).

An umbrella term for methods used to examine, copy and change genetic material. With genetic engineering, researchers can move genes between organisms - for example so that bacteria produce human insulin. The technology offers great opportunities but also raises ethical questions.
Genetically modified organism - an organism whose genetic material has been changed using genetic engineering, e.g. to produce insulin, resist disease or give a better harvest.
A small, circular DNA molecule that occurs naturally in bacteria, separate from the bacterium's chromosome. Plasmids are used in genetic engineering as vectors to introduce foreign genes into cells.
An enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific base sequence. Used in genetic engineering to cut out and paste in gene segments - a kind of molecular scissors.
DNA that contains sequences from two or more different sources, produced using restriction enzymes and ligase. The basic principle behind genetic modification.
A precise genetic tool that works like a programmable DNA scissors. CRISPR can find an exact sequence in the genome and cut or edit it - making it possible to treat genetic diseases.
Polymerase chain reaction - a method for copying a specific DNA sequence millions of times in a short period. Used in criminal investigations, disease diagnostics and research.

Methods for reading and comparing DNA, for example to establish family relationships or identify a person. Since every person's DNA is unique (except in identical twins), a DNA sample can act as a kind of fingerprint in criminal investigations and paternity tests.

Creating one or more individuals that are genetically identical to another. Since the clones have exactly the same genetic material as the original, they resemble each other like identical twins. Cloning occurs naturally in some organisms and can also be done artificially.
